claims.text: Hyperkalemia: ECG changes are frequently visible once potassium is > 5.5 mEq/L.
claims.quote: ECG changes (see figure ECG Patterns in Hyperkalemia ) are frequently visible when serum potassium is > 5.5 mEq/L (> 5.5 mmol/L).

claims.text: Early hyperkalemia: longer PR interval, shorter QT interval, and tall, symmetric, peaked T waves.
claims.quote: Slowing of conduction is characterized by an increased PR interval and shortening of the QT interval. Tall, symmetric, peaked T waves are visible initially.

claims.text: Potassium > 6.5 mEq/L: wider QRS, loss of the P wave, nodal and escape ventricular rhythms; finally a sine wave pattern, then ventricular fibrillation or asystole.
claims.quote: Potassium > 6.5 mEq/L (> 6.5 mmol/L) causes further slowing of conduction with widening of the QRS interval, disappearance of the P wave, and nodal and escape ventricular arrhythmias. Finally, the QRS complex degenerates into a sine wave pattern, and ventricular fibrillation or asystole ensues.

claims.text: Hypokalemia: cardiac effects are usually minimal until potassium is < 3 mEq/L.
claims.quote: Cardiac effects of hypokalemia are usually minimal until serum potassium concentrations are < 3 mEq/L

claims.text: Hypokalemia arrhythmias: premature ventricular and atrial beats, ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, and second- or third-degree AV block.
claims.quote: Hypokalemia may cause premature ventricular beats and premature atrial contractions , ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias , and second- or third-degree atrioventricular block .

claims.text: Significant preexisting heart disease or digoxin: even mild hypokalemia can cause conduction abnormalities.
claims.quote: Patients with significant preexisting heart disease and patients receiving digoxin are at risk of cardiac conduction abnormalities as a result of even mild hypokalemia.
